questions.tooltip: For this indicator, the scope of the GISCO reporting relates to the volume of cocoa contained in the end consumer products that your organisation / company has supplied to the German market. Conversion to MT-BE, of cocoa sourced in different forms, is to be done using the ICCO conversion factors, being: 1,33 for cocoa butter (1804); 1,25 for cocoa paste/liquor (18031); and 1,18 for cocoa powder and cake (1805, 18032). Does your organisation / company have data to report on the cocoa origin transparency for the reporting year?
questions.tooltip:
The cocoa origin transparency level concerns the level of information on the origin of cocoa being documented at the initial stage of the cocoa sourcing process, with such information remaining available at later stages of the value chain.
Distinction is made between the following origin transparency levels, for which further definitions may be found in the definition list:
  • Score 1: Origin unknown or only country of origin known
  • Score 2: Country and region of origin known
  • Score 3: Country, region and municipality / cooperative of origin known
  • Score 4: Farm known, in addition to the country, region and municipality / cooperative of origin
  • Score 5: Farm known and having point coordinates of the farm household (farm mapping)
  • Score 5+: Farm known and having polygon boundaries of the farm
  • Score 6: Farm known, having polygon boundaries of the farm and farm plots verified as not in a protected forest and as not comprising land that was deforested since 2018.
    Having a high origin transparency score still allows for mixing of beans at later stages (during transport and / or processing).
If the corresponding sourcing information cannot be disaggregated per destination (national markets in Europe), please apply the % of your organisation's global sourcing.

(Subsequently, you will be asked to provide the corresponding volumes of cocoa, expressed in % of your organization's total cocoa sourcing, per traceability category.)
questions.tooltip:
Please check the specific definitions (in the definition list) for the 5 traceability categories:
  • Conventional: Conventional cocoa is cocoa sourced without conforming to the traceability requirements of ‘mass balance’, ‘segregated’, or ‘identity preserved’ - please refer to the corresponding definitions.
  • Mass balance: The mass balance system administratively monitors the trade of conforming cocoa throughout the entire supply chain. The system requires transparent documentation and justification of the origin and quantity of conforming cocoa purchased by the first buyer. The mass balance system allows mixing conforming and nonconforming cocoa in later stages of the cocoa value chain (e.g. transport, processing, manufacturing). Cocoa value chain actors can sell a certain mass of conforming cocoa, or an equivalent volume of conforming cocoa-containing products, to the extent that the actual volumes of sales of conforming products are tracked and audited through the supply chain and providing that these volumes do not exceed the cocoa bean equivalents of conforming cocoa bought at origin. (Definition drafted using elements borrowed from ISO-CEN and Fairtrade).
  • Mass balance with country of origin preserved
  • Segregated: Certified or independently verified cocoa meeting the segregation requirements. As per the mass-balance system, segregation requires a transparent documentation and justification of the origin and quantity of conforming cocoa (this is certified or independently verified cocoa) purchased by the first buyer. Conforming cocoa is kept segregated from nonconforming cocoa, including during transport, storage, processing cocoa, and manufacturing of cocoa-containing products. Segregation does allow mixing cocoa from different origins, to the extent that all cocoa being mixed qualifies as conforming cocoa (as per the certification standard or verified company scheme being applied). The cocoa supply chain actors shall demonstrate that they have taken the required measures to avoid mixing conforming cocoa with nonconforming cocoa. (Definition drafted using elements borrowed from ISO-CEN and Rainforest Alliance).
  • Identity preserved: Identity preserved is the highest traceability type. There is no mixing of cocoa, neither with non-conforming cocoa, nor with cocoa from other origins. If the ‘single origin’ is set at cooperative level or at cocoa-producing area (combining different cooperatives), then conforming cocoa from this broader origin may be combined. In other words, the “identity preserved” system meets all requirements of “segregated cocoa” but it does not allow mixing cocoa from different origins.
Remark: If the corresponding sourcing information cannot be disaggregated per destination (national markets in Europe), please apply the % of your organisation's / company’s global sourcing per traceability category.

Does your organisation / company have information available on the average amount per ton of cocoa beans paid to the farmer (combining farm gate price + all premiums)?
questions.tooltip: As far as possible, please work with weighted averages per sourcing volume and price. Where it becomes unmanageable to weigh all sourcing volumes at their individual prices, please work with the next best estimation such as weighting by estimated country averages. To the extent possible, all organisations / companies, no matter where they are located in the supply chain, should report on this indicator, including companies with consumer brands and retailers. In order to get the relevant information, you may approach your cocoa suppliers . When the corresponding information is transferred all along the value chain / chain of custody, also consumer brands or retailers would thus be able to report on the average amounts that apply to the cocoa contained in the products they bring to the consumer market.

questions.name: Please specify the average amount (in USD) per ton of cocoa beans paid to the farmer.
questions.tooltip: This average amount per ton of cocoa beans paid to the farmer comprises: the farm gate price + all premiums paid directly to the farmer + all premiums documented as shared with the farmer by the cooperative or farmer organisation.  Amounts of premiums paid to a cooperative or farmer organisation, without knowing how much of the premium is shared with the farmer, are NOT to be reported here, but under the next indicator.  Every actor shall calculate their own “weighted average amount per ton of cocoa beans paid to the farmer”, based on the average values pertaining to their sourcing mix, for the part of the cocoa for which such information is provided to them by their suppliers.

Does your organisation / company have information available on the average amount, per ton of cocoa bean equivalents sourced, of additional funding of cooperatives and cocoa sustainability projects / programmes?
questions.tooltip: Under this indicator you can report (in the form of an average amount of funding per ton of cocoa beans sourced): all premiums paid to a cooperative and not documented as shared with the farmer; other funding provided to cooperatives or farmer organisations; other funding for cocoa sustainability projects / programmes. Any amounts of mandatory Living Income Differential (LID) paid are not to be included in this calculation. However, the member / partner can report on the LID paid under a separate question later.  Such funding for cocoa sustainability projects / programmes does include support provided to value chain actors in the countries of origin. But this funding does not include investments in the company's own operations, its own due diligence or its own sustainability reporting. You cannot claim the funding provided by third parties. To the extent possible, companies should approach their suppliers of cocoa if they are not able to provide data for this indicator. Each subsequent actor in the value chain would be able to calculate the weighted average for all its cocoa sourcing. That actor would be able to add any own cocoa sustainability funding (not comprised in what was reported by their suppliers) and thus increase a higher value for this indicator. They would be able to communicate that information to the subsequent actors in the chain of custody. You cannot claim the funding provided by third parties. You can only claim funding that benefits the cooperatives and farmers (e.g. services, expertise etc.)   The idea behind the indicator on sustainability investments is that all sustainability investments accumulate and that we have a weighted average of price paid to the farmer and of the additional sustainability investments for the cocoa supplied to the German / Belgian consumer market - Every brand / label will have its own amount that they can compare with the overall average.  All sustainability funding is to be reported related to volume.

Under this indicator you can report (in the form of an average amount of funding per ton of cocoa beans sourced):
  • all premiums paid to a cooperative and not documented as shared with the farmer
  • other funding provided to cooperatives or farmer organisations
  • other funding for cocoa sustainability projects / programmes
Any amounts of mandatory Living Income Differential (LID) paid are not to be included in this calculation. However, the member / partner can report on the LID paid under a separate question later. Such funding for cocoa sustainability projects / programmes does include support provided to value chain actors in the countries of origin. But this funding does not include investments in the company's own operations, its own due diligence or its own sustainability reporting. You cannot claim the funding provided by third parties.

question_groups.name: Value chain Due Diligence
question_groups.description:
The subsequent question block entails questions related to value chain due diligence. This covers implementation by members / partners of human rights compliance programs in the cocoa supply chain in identified risk areas and corresponding public reporting. The actors along the cocoa supply chains are expected to actively implement the 6 components of the human rights due diligence (HRDD) concept (as per UN and OECD Guiding Principles). If you select Initial stages, Intermediary level, Advanced level or Fully implemented, you will be asked to report on whether your organisation / company has implemented the different elements of the Human Rights Due Diligence (HRDD) concept. 
The same holds for Environmental Due Diligence.

question_groups.name: Child labour (DISCO)
question_groups.description: The subsequent question block entails questions related to child labour. The objective of this question block is to understand the deployment level of CLMRS in relation to the DISCO targets on rolling out CLMRS and the contributions on non-supply chain partners in the partnership to reach the goals around ending child labour.

questions.name: Do you have data available on the volume (expressed in MT-BE) of cocoa that your company sourced with a reliable claim that the cocoa is “sourced from cocoa farming households covered by a child labour monitoring & remediation system (CLMRS)”?
questions.tooltip: To qualify as a CLMRS, in alignment with the other ISCO’s, the system should meet the definition and requirements, developed by ICI. Identical tooltips will be used as for the questionnaires of the other ISCOs. A “reliable claim” means: (a) that the sustainability characteristic (in the example above “sourced from cocoa farming households household covered by a CLMRS”) is well documented at that stage of the supply chain, and (b) that measures are implemented to provide assurance on the trustworthiness of the data. A “reliable claim” does not require segregation between cacao with and cacao without this claim. As per a mass balance system, mixing is allowed, as long as assurance is being provided that the claim is passed on to cocoa containing products with an aggregated corresponding volume of cocoa bean equivalents that may not exceed the volume of cocoa beans sourced and documented with this claim at the start of the chain of custody / value chain. In other words the risk of over-claiming shall be very well mitigated.

questions.tooltip:
A “reliable claim” means:
  • (a) that the sustainability characteristic (in the example above “sourced from a whom the living income gap is calculated”) is well documented at that stage of the supply chain;

A “reliable claim” does not require segregation between cacao with and cacao without this claim. In other words the risk of over-claiming shall be very well mitigated. The supported calculation of the living income gap and the development or update of a smart mix living income strategy – referred to above, must have occurred in the past 2 years. questions.name: Does your organisation / company have data to report on volumes of cocoa processed in Germany, for which a reference price for a living income was paid to the farmer during the reporting year?
questions.tooltip:
Please note that it is mandatory to report on Côte d'Ivoire and Ghana separately. For other countries you can choose to:
  • (a) provide country-specific data per country where you sourced cocoa with a reference price for a living income;
  • (b) provide only aggregated data for those other countries.
The amount effectively paid to the farmer comprises the farmgate price, the premiums paid directly to the farmer and the premiums shared with the farmer by the cooperative. Any support in kind to the farmer is not taken into account for this indicator. Any claims of “cocoa for which a reference price for a living income was effectively paid to the farmer”, must be backed up by a chain of custody administration demonstrating the trustworthiness of the claim. This implies documentation and transparency of the sourcing details and assurance that the claim is linked to a matching volume of cocoa beans with an amount equivalent to the price effectively paid to the farmer. The country-specific Living Income Reference Price (LIRP) to be compared with are: $ 2.200 / ton for Côte d'Ivoire (as per Fairtrade LIRP); $ 2.300 / ton for Ghana (as per Fairtrade LIRP). Please note that the reference price for a living income claimed should be as high or higher as the Fairtrade LIRP. Members can introduce own calculations on reference prices. The calculation must be publicly available and should be proved by experts on a yearly basis. Thus, the payment to the farmer does not have to be done through any Fairtrade process, certification or comparable mechanism.

Any claims of “cocoa for which a reference price for a living income was effectively paid to the farmer”, must be backed up by a chain of custody administration demonstrating the trustworthiness of the claim. This implies documentation and transparency of the sourcing details and assurance that the claim is linked to a matching volume of cocoa beans with an amount equivalent to the price effectively paid to the farmer.    The country-specific Living Income Reference Price (LIRP) to be compared with are: $ 2.200 / ton for Côte d'Ivoire (as per Fairtrade LIRP); $ 2.300 / ton for Ghana (as per Fairtrade LIRP). Please note that the reference price for a living income claimed should be as high or higher as the Fairtrade LIRP.     Members can introduce own calculations on reference prices. The calculation must be publicly available and should be proved by experts on a yearly basis. Thus, the payment to the farmer does not have to be done through any Fairtrade process, certification or comparable mechanism.
